**Assertions extracted from this record:**

| Assertion | Role | Fact type | Value |
|-----------|------|-----------|-------|
| a_008 | child_2 | name | Patrick Flynn |
| a_009 | child_2 | birth | age 15, ~1845, Ireland |
| a_010 | child_2 | relationship | Listed in Thomas Flynn household, position consistent with son |

**Person_evidence links for these assertions:**

| Assertion | pe_ entry | Person | Confidence |
|-----------|-----------|--------|-----------|
| a_008 | — none — | — | — |
| a_009 | — none — | — | — |
| a_010 | pe_004 | I1 (Patrick Flynn) | confident |

**Gaps identified:**

**Gap 1 — a_008 and a_009 are entirely unlinked.**
Only a_010 (the relationship assertion) was linked to I1. The name assertion (a_008) and the birth assertion (a_009) for the same persona (`child_2`) carry no `pe_` links at all. They should each link to I1 on the same basis as a_010, since all three assertions belong to the same persona. Leaving the name and birth assertions unlinked means the 1860 census contributes no name or birth facts through the person_evidence chain — a gap in the evidentiary record.

**Gap 2 — a_010 has only one-sided `pe_` links: the Thomas Flynn (I2) side is missing.**
a_010 is a relationship assertion. Its `structured_value` explicitly names `head_of_household` as the related person role, and the source's citation confirms this is the Thomas Flynn household. The assertion bears on both Patrick (I1) and Thomas Flynn (I2) — exactly the bilateral cardinality rule. pe_004 covers I1, but there is no corresponding `pe_` entry linking a_010 to I2. This is the single most common incompleteness pattern the skill is designed to catch: the other party's link was not written.

Compare the 1850 census: assertion a_004 (the parallel relationship assertion from that record) was correctly linked to both I1 (pe_002) and I2 (pe_006). The 1860 record's relationship assertion should have received the same treatment but did not.

**Gap 3 — No head_of_household persona assertions extracted.**
The record's citation explicitly names "Thomas Flynn household," but no assertions were extracted for a `head_of_household` role. That means there is no `pe_` link connecting the 1860 census to Thomas Flynn (I2) at all — not through any assertion. By contrast, the 1850 census has a_005 (head of household name assertion) linked to I2 via pe_003. The 1860 census should have an equivalent assertion linking Thomas Flynn's presence in that year to his tree person. This is likely a record-extraction gap rather than a person-evidence gap, but it surfaces here as a missing link: I2 has no connection to this record.

**Summary of gaps:**

| Gap | What is missing | Severity |
|-----|----------------|----------|
| a_008 → I1 | pe_ link for Patrick's name assertion in 1860 census | Missing |
| a_009 → I1 | pe_ link for Patrick's birth assertion in 1860 census | Missing |
| a_010 → I2 | pe_ link for Thomas Flynn on the 1860 relationship assertion | Missing |
| head_of_household assertions | No assertions extracted for Thomas Flynn in 1860 at all | Likely extraction gap |

**Calibration note on pe_004.**
The existing link (a_010 → I1, `confident`) has no `match_score` recorded. The rationale is adequate — it cites age consistency with 1850 and same county — but it omits whether `same_person` was called. The `match_score: null` may be correct if the 1860 census persona had no reachable record document for scoring, but the rationale should state that explicitly. As written, it is not possible to tell whether the score was deliberately skipped or simply never obtained. This is a calibration note, not a disqualifying problem.

The warnings are all of the same type: "An event is dated more than 2 years before this person's latest birth-like fact." This is a pre-existing coherence issue from earlier sources (S1, S2) that were already on the tree before this run — the 1841 and 1851 Residence facts exist from the prior records (src_001/src_002 are labelled the Utah censuses, while the English census records appear to have been on the tree already under S1/S2). These warnings are not introduced by this run's links; they reflect that the persons have approximate birth years derived from age-reporting (~1822, ~1825, etc.) while the 1841/1851 English residence facts predate the birth-year estimates by enough to trigger the check. This is a known artifact of census-derived approximate birth years and is not a genealogical impossibility — the approximate birth year could simply be slightly off (age rounding in censuses was common). These warnings pre-existed this run and are not new.

---

The 1860 and 1880 Salt Lake County census records have been fully linked to the family tree. Here is what was done:

**1860 Census (src_001) — 4 personas linked:**
- head (Joseph Pratt, ~1822, England) → I1 (Joseph Pratt): confident, score 0.78
- household_member_1 (Ann Pratt, ~1825, England) → I2 (Ann Pratt): confident, score 0.78
- household_member_2 (Sarah Pratt, ~1847, England) → I3 (Sarah Pratt): confident, score 0.78
- household_member_3 (Joseph Pratt, ~1850, England) → I4 (Joseph Pratt Jr.): confident, score 0.78

**1880 Census (src_002) — 3 personas linked:**
- head (Joseph Pratt, ~1822, England) → I1: confident, score 0.78
- wife (Ann Pratt, ~1825, England) → I2: confident, score 0.78
- son (Joseph Pratt, ~1850, England) → I4: confident, score 0.78

**Person_evidence entries created:** pe_001 through pe_020 (20 entries, covering all assertions including both-sided links for relationship assertions).

**Facts materialized:** Residence and birth facts from both censuses written onto I1, I2, I3, and I4. No conflicts surfaced.

**Household check:** Sarah (I3) is present in 1860 but absent from the 1880 household. At ~33 years old in 1880 she would likely be married and in her own household — this is plausible and not a red flag.

**Geographic move:** England to Utah is a documented emigration corridor explicitly named on the FamilySearch Utah Emigration and Immigration wiki: "Many Latter-day Saint immigrants leaving Europe and Great Britain came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England" (1840-1890 era). This bridges the move and supports confident links.

**Warnings noted:** All four persons show a pre-existing coherence flag about events dated before estimated birth years — this arises from the approximate (~1822, ~1825, etc.) birth years derived from census age-reporting and is not introduced by this run.

---

Both census records very confidently match Joseph Pratt and his family in Salt Lake County, Utah. The 1860 record shows Joseph (about 38) and Ann (about 35) with their children Sarah (13) and young Joseph (10), all born in England. Twenty years later the 1880 record finds the same couple still in the same county, now with their son Joseph still living with them as an adult of about 30 — Sarah had apparently married and moved to her own household by then, which is entirely normal.

The next step for this project would be proof-conclusion: gathering the evidence across all linked records to write a formal conclusion answering question q_001 — whether these are definitively the subject's family — and then searching for additional records such as a naturalization, land deed, or church membership that could document the family's emigration from England to Utah.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The proof summary (ps_001) recognizes and resolves this conflict under the label c_001. But **pe_005 does not mention it at all**, and does not carry a `core_identifier_conflict` field entry.

Under the match threshold policy, any core identifier — birthplace qualifies — that contradicts what the tree person already attests must be declared in `core_identifier_conflict`. The policy is explicit: *"If one does, put it in the entry's `core_identifier_conflict` field, naming both sides."* The field may be left null (or cleared to null with a reason) only when *"the conflict is explained and does not bear on identity."*

Here, the conflict has in fact been explained and resolved: ps_001 adjudicates it well, preferring Ireland and attributing the Pennsylvania entry to informant error. That resolution means the conflict does not bear on identity and the field can legitimately be null — **but the rationale must say so**. pe_005's rationale is silent on the conflict, as if it does not exist.

---

### Step 3: The informant quality problem and the confidence ceiling

a_013 is the relationship assertion ("Father: Thomas Flynn"), not the death event itself. Its informant is James Brown, son-in-law, `family_not_present`, `information_quality: secondary`. The `informant_bias_notes` state: *"Secondary information — son-in-law reporting what he was told about father-in-law's parentage."*

pe_005's rationale states: *"Names match, death location matches known residence."* That reasoning applies to the death event (a_011, whose informant is the attending physician — `witness`, `primary`), not to a_013. The link in pe_005 is to the **relationship** assertion a_013, whose provenance is secondary. The rationale has effectively borrowed the attending physician's credibility for a fact the physician did not report.

However — and this is important — confidence in a pe_ link measures **identity certainty** (is this record about I1?), not the quality of the individual assertion. A secondary informant on the father's name does not automatically lower the identity confidence for the deceased. The record is about Patrick Flynn who died in 1908 in Schuylkill County: that identification is strong. The secondary informant matters for how much weight to place on "Thomas Flynn" as the father's name, not directly for whether the deceased is I1.

This means the confidence-calibration question is separable from the informant-quality point: but pe_005 conflates the two by presenting the informant-quality note as if it were an identity argument. The rationale should have been explicit that the `confident` tier rests on the identity of the deceased (name, location, year), not on the quality of the parentage claim in a_013.

---

### Step 4: The missing match_score

pe_005 has `match_score: null`. Under the policy, null is appropriate only when "no record persona is reachable" or "the candidate was minted from the persona itself." Neither applies here. The record has a `deceased` persona (record_id `ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF`), and I1 is not a stub minted from this record — I1 was first established from the 1850 census. A `same_person` call for this pairing was both possible and required, and no score was obtained. This is a score discipline failure.

---

### Step 5: Is `confident` justified overall?

Working through the match threshold:

- **Identity-level evidence:** Name, year of death, and county of death all match I1 without any competitor — there is no plausible alternative Patrick Flynn dying in Schuylkill County in 1908. The other pe_ links (pe_001, pe_004) are already `confident` on records with the same county and consistent ages. The death certificate's own primary-informant facts (a_011, death event, attending physician) strongly corroborate identity. This is a **strong** match on identity.
- **Birthplace conflict:** Exists but is resolved by ps_001 (the conflict is adjudicated in the proof summary, attributable to informant error). The resolution is documented, though pe_005 does not acknowledge it.
- **No geographic move:** The death certificate is in Schuylkill County, the same county as every prior link. The residence-cluster check is satisfied trivially.
- **No core identifier that remains unresolved:** The birthplace conflict is resolved; no other identifier conflicts.

On the strength of the qualitative identity match alone — same name, same county, same approximate birth year, no competing candidate, consistent with two earlier censuses — `confident` is qualitatively defensible. The identity of the deceased is not in serious doubt.

---

### Conclusion of the Review

**The `confident` tier is defensible on the merits**, but pe_005 is poorly documented in three ways that would fail a rigorous audit:

1. **The rationale is thin.** It reads like a summary of the record's content rather than an identity argument. It does not name the specific corroborating pe_ links (pe_001, pe_004) that establish I1's profile across two censuses, it does not explain how the death year and location place the deceased within the same identity cluster, and it makes no mention of the absence of a competing candidate.

2. **The birthplace conflict (Ireland vs. Pennsylvania) is not acknowledged.** Even though the conflict is resolved in ps_001 (c_001), pe_005 should note that the conflict exists and that it was adjudicated in the proof summary with Ireland preferred. The rationale should explicitly state the conflict does not undermine identity and cite the resolution — otherwise a future reviewer cannot tell whether the conflict was considered or simply missed.

3. **No `same_person` score was obtained.** The persona was reachable; the call was required and was not made. The score should be disclosed in both the `match_score` field and the rationale prose, per the policy.

**Recommended rationale (for user authorization before any update is made):**

> "Date check: death cert birth year 1845 vs. I1 tree birth year ~1845 (derived from 1850 census, age 5): gap 0 years. Residence check: Schuylkill County, PA 1908 vs. Schuylkill County, PA 1860 (pe_004, nearest attested residence): same county. Patrick Flynn, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, is the only Patrick Flynn of approximately this age dying in that county in that year. Name, death year, and death county are all consistent with the same individual established by pe_001 (1850 census) and pe_004 (1860 census), which together fix I1 in Schuylkill County from at least 1850 through 1860. No competing candidate exists. A birthplace conflict exists — the death certificate states Pennsylvania while both censuses state Ireland — but this conflict has been adjudicated in the project proof summary (ps_001, c_001) as informant error by the son-in-law James Brown, and does not affect the identity of the deceased. [Score: same_person not called — required, see note.] Confidence: confident on identity of the deceased."

The three concerns above are material enough that I would recommend asking the user to authorize (a) running `same_person` for this pairing to obtain and disclose the score, and (b) updating the rationale text to reflect the above before the entry is relied upon in proof-conclusion.

No writes have been made in this review.

---

The 1908 death certificate almost certainly does refer to the same Patrick Flynn who is tree person I1 — the evidence for that identity is strong. The person-evidence agent has successfully linked the 1908 death certificate's (src_004) unlinked assertions to Patrick Flynn (I1). Here's a summary of what was done:

- **pe_007**: Assertion a_011 (death, 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County) → Patrick Flynn (I1), confident

- The death fact was added to I1.
- The birth fact gained a second source reference.

The coherence warning about two coexisting Birth facts on I1 is a known, expected conflict — not a chronological impossibility.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly identified the geographic gap (Horsham, Sussex to Maury County, Tennessee, 6,804 km) and applied the decided rule: capping all links at `probable` rather than `confident`. All 12 person_evidence entries were written with `probable` confidence and rationales explicitly naming the gap. The same_person scores (0.78) were obtained and recorded. Facts were materialized with proper source references. Relationship edges were written with source assertions. The skill recovered cleanly from an initial validation rejection that required confidence downgrade and same_person scoring. No fabricated material; all claims are grounded in the sources and tool responses.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed all required work: linked both census records (1870 and 1880) to the five tree persons (I1–I5); created 12 person_evidence entries covering all household members and relationship assertions; materialized facts from both censuses; wrote three relationship edges (Couple I1–I2, ParentChild I1–I5, ParentChild I2–I5); called same_person for all scorable assertions; and flagged the absence of James and Ellen in the 1880 census as an identity question. No major portions were omitted.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. same_person calls used correct assertionId and treePersonId pairs; recordRole was correctly omitted for the assertion's own party (head, wife, son) and correctly supplied only for the second party in relationship assertions (e.g., recordRole: 'head' when linking I1 to a_019 wife assertion). materialize_facts calls matched persons to record roles correctly. tree_edit calls used relationship-establishing assertions (a_019, a_020) as sourceAssertionId, not name assertions. The skill recovered from a validation rejection by removing unsourced edges (I1→I3, I1→I4, I2→I3, I2→I4) and resubmitting with only the three edges that had relationship-assertion provenance. No fixture_not_found errors.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 12 person_evidence entries are scored `probable`, which is correct for this scenario. The decided rule caps unexplained moves outside the residence cluster at `probable`, never `confident`. The skill correctly applied this cap: despite a high same_person score (0.78) and strong name/age/household correlation across two independent censuses, the geographic gap (Horsham, Sussex to Maury County, Tennessee, with no documentary bridge or corridor) prevents `confident`. The rationales explicitly name the gap, the distance (6,804 km), and the absence of a corridor on the Tennessee wiki page. No `speculative` was used (which would over-apply the rule). The confidence tier matches the identity-evidence strength.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: name matches exactly (e.g., 'William Weller'), age consistent with birth year (e.g., 'age 45 in 1870 gives ~1825'), birthplace England, household position (head, wife, son, child), and cross-record corroboration where applicable (e.g., George appears in both 1870 and 1880). Critically, every rationale addresses the geographic gap: names the two places (Maury County, Tennessee vs. Horsham, Sussex), states the distance (6,804 km), and notes the absence of a documentary bridge or corridor. The rationales explain why the link is `probable` rather than `confident` despite the strong correlation. Competing candidates are not explicitly ruled out, but the scenario provides no competing candidates, so this is not a deficiency.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: For every relationship-implying assertion, both person_evidence entries exist. The 1880 wife relationship (a_019) is linked to both I2 (wife) and I1 (head) via pe_009 and pe_010. The 1880 son relationship (a_020) is linked to both I5 (son) and I1 (head) via pe_011 and pe_012. The Couple edge (I1–I2) and ParentChild edges (I1→I5, I2→I5) were written via tree_edit with source-refs from the relationship assertions. The skill correctly recognized that name assertions (a_001, a_003, a_005, a_007, a_009, a_012, a_014, a_016) do not establish relationships and do not require two-sided links.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: All five persons (I1–I5) already existed in the tree; no new persons were minted. The skill correctly linked existing persons to the census assertions via person_evidence and materialized facts from both censuses with resolved source-refs (S10 for 1870, S11 for 1880). Relationship edges were written via tree_edit with source-refs from relationship-establishing assertions (a_019 for Couple, a_020 for ParentChild). The skill did not attempt to mint new persons or overwrite existing tree persons. The merge_warnings gate was not invoked (no candidate record document was in hand; the scenario was built from pre-extracted assertions), and this was correctly handled. Confidence was calibrated to the evidence (single source with geographic gap → `probable`, not `confident`). match_score was recorded from same_person calls (0.78 for all).

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for all 12 assertions (8 name assertions + 4 relationship assertions). Each call was scored and the score (0.78) was recorded in match_score. The score informed but did not override the correlation analysis: despite the high score, the geographic gap capped confidence at `probable`. recordRole was correctly omitted for the assertion's own party (head, wife, son) and correctly supplied for the second party in relationship assertions (recordRole: 'head' when linking I1 to a_019 and a_020). The score was treated as an input that informs the confidence tier, not as a verdict that replaces it. No circular scoring occurred (the persons were not minted from these very records).
